title: My Sister and I Gave Birth on the Same Day, but Our Parents Celebrated Her Son for Nine Hours Without Visiting Me—Then I Discovered Their Secret Plan for My House
excerpt: My Sister and I Gave Birth on the Same Day, but Our Parents Celebrated Her Son for Nine Hours Without Visiting Me—Then I Discovered Their Secret Plan for My Hou...
author: admin

blocks.text: My name is Odalie, and I’d always known my younger sister, Medelli, was our parents’ favorite.

I had spent most of my childhood pretending it didn’t bother me. When Medelli received expensive birthday presents, I told myself she was younger. When she made mistakes, I told myself our parents were simply more patient with her. When my achievements were overlooked, I convinced myself that being independent was something to be proud of.
But I never imagined their favoritism would become so obvious on the day we both became mothers.
By an extraordinary coincidence, Medelli and I delivered our babies in the same hospital, just two rooms apart.
I gave birth to a beautiful little girl.
My husband, Daniel, held my hand throughout the delivery. When the nurse placed our daughter in my arms, I forgot about everything else.
I was still recovering when Daniel called my parents to share the wonderful news.
Then she asked whether Medelli had delivered yet.
Daniel explained that both babies had arrived safely.
Mom barely responded before saying, “We’ll come see you later, sweetheart. We’re just helping your sister settle in.”
After all, this was my first child. Surely my parents would want to meet their granddaughter.
Every time I heard footsteps outside my room, I looked toward the door.
Meanwhile, photographs kept appearing in our family group chat.
My parents standing beside Medelli’s hospital bed, smiling proudly.
There were balloons, flowers, and even a large box of chocolates.
The caption beneath one photograph read:
“Our first grandson! Our family is finally complete!”
I stared at those words for a long time.
Finally, I picked up my phone and called Dad.
“Dad, I just wanted to know if you were coming to see Amelia.”
Then he snapped, “WE’RE EXHAUSTED! Do you know how long we’ve been here? Your sister needs us right now!”
“We’ll visit when we have time, Odalie.”
Daniel noticed my expression and gently squeezed my hand.
“Don’t let this ruin today,” he said. “Our daughter has everything she needs. She has us.”
I nodded, although the disappointment was difficult to hide.
I thought that was the worst thing that would happen that day.
Around twenty minutes later, a nurse named Patricia entered my room.
She checked Amelia’s identification bracelet and reviewed some paperwork.
“Mrs. Odalie, I need to ask you something.”
“Has anyone in your family contacted the hospital about your daughter’s discharge arrangements?”
“Someone approached the maternity desk earlier. They wanted to know when Amelia would be released, whether another relative could collect her, and whether the discharge address could be changed.”
“They didn’t provide a clear explanation. They said they were close family members and wanted to help.”
“I haven’t authorized anyone to collect my daughter. Only my husband and I are handling her discharge.”
“That’s what we needed to confirm. We’ll make sure no changes are made without your direct authorization.”
After she left, I felt strangely unsettled.
Why would anyone be asking those questions?
He said he was returning from the cafeteria.
A few minutes later, he walked through the door.
He wasn’t carrying his usual coffee, and his expression was unusually serious.
“Well, at least they finally remembered they have another daughter.”
“They were talking to Medelli. I didn’t want to interrupt, but I overheard something about our house.”
“Your father said everything needed to be arranged before we brought Amelia home. Your mother said the paperwork was almost ready. Then Medelli asked whether we would find out.”
“I managed to photograph something on the table.”
The house Daniel and I had purchased together three years earlier.
And beside the property details was a signature that looked remarkably like mine.
My eyes moved to the proposed recipient’s name.
“I don’t know yet. But your father said they intended to convince you to sign the remaining documents after you were discharged.”
Then another detail caught my attention.
Daniel and I had worked hard for that house.
We had saved for years, sacrificed vacations, and carefully planned our finances. It wasn’t a mansion, but it was ours.
My parents knew how much it meant to us.
For the past several months, Dad had repeatedly complained about his financial problems.
The second time, Daniel and I agreed that we couldn’t keep covering his expenses.
Now I understood why he had suddenly become interested in our property.
But I still couldn’t understand why Medelli was involved.
Please don’t make things difficult. Mom and Dad are trying to help everyone.
How exactly was secretly transferring my house to my sister supposed to help me?
Daniel suggested we contact our property lawyer immediately.
